extracted.intended_audience: professional indexers, copyeditors, authors, and publishers preparing book or journal indexes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for creating, formatting, and alphabetizing indexes for books and journal volumes, including rules for names, places, punctuation, subentries, use of proofs, and indexing workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing systems (letter-by-letter vs word-by-word)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two systems for alphabetizing index entries are described and compared: letter-by-letter and word-by-word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both systems ignore most punctuation and treat parentheses or commas as interruptions. Choose one system (publisher preference) and apply consistently; see examples and note differences in ordering behavior between the two systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of precedence for same initial words
rubrics_metrics.description: When headings share the same starting word, the order of precedence is: one word, word followed by a parenthesis, word followed by a comma, word followed by a space, then (ignoring other punctuation) word followed by a number, and word followed by letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this sequence when ordering entries such as NEW (…), New, Arthur, new-12 compound, newborn, newcomer, etc.; see illustrated columns for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses and commas interrupt alphabetizing; other punctuation ignored
rubrics_metrics.description: A parenthesis or comma (in that order) interrupts alphabetizing; hyphens, slashes, quotation marks, periods, and similar punctuation are ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this rule across both letter-by-letter and word-by-word systems; consult specific sections (e.g., 16.61) for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of ampersand (&) and at sign (@)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ampersand may be treated as if spelled out; an at sign, which normally can be treated like the letter a, may be ignored as part of a screen name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are two explicit exceptions to general punctuation treatment; follow publisher preference and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing headings beginning with numerals (isolated entries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated entries beginning with numerals are alphabetized as though spelled out (e.g., 1984 alphabetized as nineteen eighty-four).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For numerals in the middle of a heading, see other rules; if many numerals occur, consider listing them together numerically at the start of the index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing similar headings containing numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more similar headings with numerals occur together, they are ordered numerically, regardless of how they would be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order entries like Henry III, Henry IV, Henry V numerically within the letter section; such entries may be placed at the beginning of that letter section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing accented letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Words beginning with or including accented letters are alphabetized as though they were unaccented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recommendation is for English-language indexes containing some non-English words; for indexes with many non-English terms consult Unicode collation specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing items with the same name across persons/places/things
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person, a place, and a thing have the same name, arrange them in normal alphabetical order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use common-sense adjustments if needed (e.g., to keep personal names together or logical); provide cross-references when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing initials versus spelled-out names
rubrics_metrics.description: Initials used in place of a given name come before any spelled-out name beginning with the same letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Oppenheimer, J. Robert comes before Oppenheimer, James N.; apply letter-by-letter ordering for initials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing abbreviations and acronyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Acronyms, initialisms, and most abbreviations are alphabetized as they appear, not according to their spelled-out versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermix abbreviations among regular entries alphabetically; see other sections for special-case exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disregarding introductory articles/prepositions/conjunctions in subentries
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductory articles, prepositions, and conjunctions are disregarded when alphabetizing subentries (except where noted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies whether subentries are run in or indented; to preserve keyword logic, avoid beginning subheadings with substantive introductory words (e.g., 'relations with').

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing subentries for indented style (invert or dispense with introductory words)
rubrics_metrics.description: In indented indexes, it may be better to dispense with introductory words or to invert headings and amplify them as needed to preserve visual alphabetic logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example conversion shown: Churchill, Winston: as anti-Fascist, Curzon line, views on, de Gaulle, relations with -> Churchill, Winston (indented) anti-Fascism of; Curzon line, views on; de Gaulle, relations with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical order of subentries
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional subentries demand numerical order even if others in the same index are alphabetized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numeric ordering for items like numbered political terms or level indicators (e.g., Daley, Richard J.: third term, fourth term).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological order of subentries (use with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a run-in index, subentries for a biography may be arranged chronologically rather than alphabetically to provide a quick summary of career events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this only when the biographical and chronological logic is obvious; avoid misuse that confuses readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing names with particles (de, van, al, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: When family names contain particles, consider the individual's preference and traditional/national usages for alphabetization; cross-references are often advisable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult authoritative references (e.g., Merriam-Webster) for well-known persons; exercise editorial discretion for names like Charles de Gaulle (Chicago prefers 'de Gaulle').

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing compound family names
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound family names, with or without hyphens, are usually alphabetized according to the first element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related guidance for exceptions and cross-references; consult sections on inversion and cultural practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing names beginning with Mac, Mc, or O'
rubrics_metrics.description: Names beginning with Mac or Mc are alphabetized letter by letter as they appear; names beginning with O' are alphabetized as if the apostrophe were missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided (Macalister, MacAlister, McAllister; Onassis, O’Neill, Ongaro); maintain letter-by-letter ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing names with 'Saint' (Saint, St., Sainte, San)
rubrics_metrics.description: A family name in the form of a saint’s name is alphabetized letter by letter as the name is spelled, whether Saint, San, St., or Ste.; cross-references may be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sainte-Beuve, Saint-Gaudens, St. Laurent; consider cross-refs like 'Saint. See St.' when entries are far apart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Arabic names
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern Arabic names (given names followed by surname) present no problem; surnames prefixed by al or el are alphabetized under the element following the particle; Abu, Abd, and Ibn are integral elements and are alphabetized under them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide cross-references if the intended readership may be unfamiliar with Arabic naming; e.g., 'al-Farabi. See Farabi, al-'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Burmese names
rubrics_metrics.description: Burmese persons usually use only a given name (one or more elements) and should be indexed under the first element; respectful terms (U, Daw) are omitted or follow in the index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Aung San Suu Kyi alphabetized under A; Thant, U under T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Chinese names
rubrics_metrics.description: Index Chinese names as spelled in the work (Pinyin or Wade-Giles). Chinese usage places family name first, so names are not inverted and no comma is used; if a person has adopted Western order, invert with a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide cross-references only if alternative forms are used in the text; examples: Li Bai (Pinyin) under L; Kung, H. H. (westernized) under K with inversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Hungarian names
rubrics_metrics.description: In Hungarian usage the family name precedes the given name; in English contexts such names are usually inverted and should be reinverted with a comma in the index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bartok Béla becomes Bartok, Béla in the index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Indian names
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern Indian names generally appear with the family name last and are indexed accordingly; personal preference and usage should be observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example entries: Gandhi, Mohandas Karamchand; query author when uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Indonesian names
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage varies: some Indonesians use only a single given name; others use multiple names. Names with Muslim or other elements may be indexed by the final element with inversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ascertain how the person's full name is referred to in the text and which element is used for short reference; consult the author if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Japanese names
rubrics_metrics.description: In Japanese usage the family name precedes the given name and names are therefore not inverted in the index; if the name is westernized in the text, it may be inverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistent treatment based on how names appear in the text; example: Tajima Yumiko: alphabetize under T; Kurosawa, Noriaki if text uses westernized order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Korean names
rubrics_metrics.description: Korean usage places the family name first; index names as presented so the family name appears first, unless the person is presented in westernized order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Kim Dae-jung under K; reinvert or index with comma when text refers to the person in western order (Lee, Chang-rae).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Portuguese names
rubrics_metrics.description: Portuguese practice indexes surnames by the last element (not by the first), except that Filho, Neto, and Junior always follow the second family name and are not treated as primary entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Portuguese and Spanish names appear together, cross-references may be necessary; examples: Camara Junior, José; Mattoso Silva Neto, Serafim da.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Spanish names
rubrics_metrics.description: In Spain and some Latin American countries a double family name is used (father’s family name first, mother’s second) and such names are alphabetized under the first element; the particle 'de' may be ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide cross-references when the person is generally known by the second element or when unsure; married women should be alphabetized by their first family name (father's).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Thai names
rubrics_metrics.description: Though family names exist in Thailand, individuals are often known by given names (first element) and the name is often alphabetized under the first name; practice varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek expert help if uncertain (examples given: Sarit Thanarat or Thanarat, Sarit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing Vietnamese names
rubrics_metrics.description: Vietnamese names commonly consist of three elements with the family name first; because individuals are often referred to by the last part of their given names, indexers are advised to index under that form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-references to the full form when appropriate (e.g., Diem, Ngo Dinh; cross-reference under Ngo Dinh Diem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing other Asian names and multicultural derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Names throughout Asia may derive from Arabic, Chinese, European languages, etc.; care must be taken to follow the usage in the text and the cultural practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When standard reference works do not supply an answer, query the author; be alert to titles and honorifics appearing as part of the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of initial article in organization names
rubrics_metrics.description: When indexing organizations whose names begin with 'the' (lowercased in running text), omit the article in the index entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Beatles (band); University of Chicago; Unicode Consortium (omit 'The').

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing personal names used as corporate names
rubrics_metrics.description: When a personal name is used as a corporate or business name, the full personal name is not inverted; alphabetize the corporate name under the first name or initials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A. G. Edwards & Sons, Inc. alphabetized under A; use cross-references where the company is widely known under a family name (John G. Shedd Aquarium. See Shedd Aquarium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Index persons and their companies separately
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal name and the name of that person’s company should be indexed separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide separate entries and cross-references where appropriate (example: Morgan, Junius S. and J. S. Morgan & Company).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing place names beginning with generic elements (Mount, Lake, Isle, Sea of)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names of mountains, lakes, etc., that begin with a generic name are usually inverted and alphabetized under the nongeneric name (e.g., McKinley, Mount; Geneva, Lake).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Islands and cities with topographic elements may be alphabetized under the first element depending on convention (Isle of Pines; Mount Vernon, NY).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing place names beginning with 'The' or non-English articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial 'the' used informally with place-names is omitted in indexing unless it is formally part of the name (e.g., The Hague is usually indexed under Hague); non-English definite articles such as El, Le, La are alphabetized according to the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hague, The; El Paso is under E; provide cross-references if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing place names beginning with 'Saint' forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Place names beginning with Saint, Sainte, St., or Ste. should be indexed as they appear in the text; use cross-references where helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French hyphenations and abbreviations should match the text (Saint-Cloud; St. Louis); be consistent with abbreviation usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma usage in index entries
rubrics_metrics.description: In run-in and indented indexes, when a main heading is followed immediately by locators, a comma appears before the first locator; commas also separate multiple locators and appear when a heading is an inversion or is qualified without subentries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lighthouses, early history of, 40-42; use commas consistently and follow alphabetizing punctuation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon usage before subheadings in run-in indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: In a run-in index, a colon appears before the first subheading when a main heading is followed immediately by subentries; in indented style, no punctuation is used after the main heading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also use a colon in cross-references to a subentry; format examples are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon separates run-in subentries and multiple cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: When subentries or sub-subentries are run in, they are separated by semicolons; multiple cross-references are also separated by semicolons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure correct run-in punctuation for readability (example given for astronomy: Galileo’s works on, 20-21, 22-23, 24; skills needed in, 548-49).

rubrics_metrics.name: Period usage in index entries
rubrics_metrics.description: In a run-in index a period is used only before 'See' or 'See under' or 'See also'; in an indented index a period is used only before 'See.' No period follows the final word of any entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a see/see also reference in parentheses follows a subheading, no period is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses in index headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses enclose identification or supplementary information in headings and affect alphabetizing (they interrupt alphabetizing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Charles I (king of England) vs Charles I (king of Portugal); apply parenthesis-interrupt rules when ordering entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dash usage for sub-subentries
rubrics_metrics.description: An em dash may be used in run-in indexes that require occasional sub-subentries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See examples for run-in formatting where sub-subentries are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: En dash usage for page ranges and inclusive locators
rubrics_metrics.description: The en dash is used for page ranges and all other inclusive locators (e.g., 'dogs, 135-42').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the manual's rules for abbreviating inclusive numbers and consult related sections for consistent numeric formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing schedule and time estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexing is intensive and time-consuming; an index for a 300-page book could take as much as three weeks or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan scheduling accordingly and consult related scheduling guidance (see 16.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing from page proofs and preferred file formats
rubrics_metrics.description: For printed works, indexers should have a clean and complete set of proofs showing final pagination; a searchable PDF is generally more helpful than a printout for searching terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For journal volumes begin when the first issue is paginated; for electronic formats additional considerations apply (linked entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult publisher's indexing preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Before beginning, indexers must know the publisher’s preferences for alphabetizing, run-in or indented style, inclusive numbers, numeric headings, and overall index length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If length is constrained, adjust indexing depth accordingly; follow house style for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing tools and software
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedicated indexing programs automate cross-referencing and collation and offer alphabetizing options but require learning time; many indexers still use word processors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using word processors, cross-references and alphabetizing must be checked manually; consult American Society for Indexing for up-to-date tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using electronic files cannot fully auto-generate an index
rubrics_metrics.description: A searchable PDF can help double-check instances of terms, but an index cannot be automatically generated from it; rereading the whole work is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate PDFs or use them to supplement manual indexing; do not rely solely on automatic extraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting index manuscript (run-in vs indented; flush-and-hang)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult the publisher to determine run-in or indented style and format the manuscript accordingly using a flush-and-hang style for entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow specified formatting and include any publisher-required headnotes or legend for typographic markers (e.g., t for table).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to begin indexing (pagination and exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexing should not begin until pagination is final (page proofs); exceptions include indexes using paragraph or section locators or electronic linked entries where earlier work may be possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors preparing their own indexes may compile term lists beforehand but should avoid doing excessive indexing that causes duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: what parts of the work to index
rubrics_metrics.description: Index the entire text of a book or article, including substantive content in notes; much front matter (title page, dedication, lists, acknowledgments) is not indexable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index substantive prefaces and introductions; appendixes should be indexed if they supplement the text but not if they merely reproduce documents; glossaries and bibliographies are usually not indexed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing footnotes and endnotes (substantive vs reference notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes should be indexed only if they continue or amplify discussion in the text (substantive notes); notes that merely cite sources (reference notes) need not be indexed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply editorial judgment to include notes that add substantive content worth indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endnote locator formatting (use of 'n' and 'nn')
rubrics_metrics.description: Endnotes are referred to by page, the letter 'n' (for note), and the note number with no internal space (e.g., 334n14); use 'nn' and an en dash for consecutive ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For notes on the same page from more than one chapter, include chapter numbers in parentheses to avoid confusion (e.g., 334n2 (chap. 8), 334n2 (chap. 9)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote locator rules (omitting note number when single on page)
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes are generally referred to like endnotes; when a footnote is the only one on the page, the note number may be omitted; do not omit numbers when several notes appear on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If text and footnote are connected, cite only the page; if not, cite both page and note (example: 156, 156n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing notes that span more than one page
rubrics_metrics.description: For endnotes or footnotes continuing onto another page, normally only the first page number is given unless the reference is specifically to material on the second page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For successive notes use inclusive page numbers and note ranges as appropriate (e.g., 234-35nn19-23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing parenthetical text citations and authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Parenthetical author-date citations are not normally indexed unless the citation documents an otherwise unattributed statement; any author discussed in text should be indexed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some fields it is customary to index every author named—check publisher or disciplinary norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author indexes: entries for cited authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Make separate entries for each author whose name appears in the text; do not index names concealed under 'et al.' in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ambiguity arises between forms of the same author name, resolve via reference list or queries; examples demonstrate formatting for multiple-author citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing illustrations, tables, charts, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative matter may be indexed if important to the discussion; references to illustrations may be set in italics or denoted by t (table), f (figure), pl (plate) etc., with an appropriate headnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References usually follow in page order; if an illustration number is essential, use 'table' or 'fig.' with no comma after the page number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning the marking and entry process (highlighting proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: After surveying the table of contents and the work, begin highlighting terms on proofs that will serve as main headings or subheadings; many indexers mark one section at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a PDF to search for terms; enter and alphabetize marked terms by section before proceeding; include notes in the same pass (see 16.110).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding how many terms to mark (guideline counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of terms to mark depends on the work: about five references per text page yields a modest index (~1/50 the length of text); fifteen or more yields a fairly long index (~1/20).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If publisher budgets limit index length, adjust marking accordingly; err on the side of inclusiveness because it's easier to drop entries than add them later.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to mark index entries on proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark principal headings, inversions for personal names, proposed subheads/modifications, and first names in margins when needed; use a colon on proofs to separate proposed principal heading and subheading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show marking for names, works, and thematic terms; be consistent and preserve provisional subheadings for later editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning and recording index subentries (use modifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each term marked, write a modification (a word or phrase) that narrows the heading as a potential subentry so the main heading is not followed only by a long string of numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modifications may be altered as indexing proceeds; keep provisional subentries to ensure useful, substantive entries rather than number-only lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording inclusive locators for multi-page discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a discussion extends over more than one page/section/paragraph, record both beginning and ending locators according to the locator system in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow rules for inclusive numbers and pagination (see 16.12 and 16.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typing and modifying index entries (three core elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most entries will include three elements: heading, modification (provisional subentry), and locator; while typing expect to modify headings, subheads, and locators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After typing each entry, read it carefully against page proofs to confirm correctness of locators and wording; retain marked proofs for reference until publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing entries during the indexing process
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexers may alphabetize as they type or let software do it, but must have decided whether to use letter-by-letter or word-by-word ordering and be prepared to switch only with publisher agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check alphabetical order manually or via software options that can exclude characters; see sections on systems (16.58-61).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final check of indexed proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: After typing all entries, read quickly through marked proofs to see whether anything indexable has been omitted; remedy omissions at this stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for terms that became significant as themes developed in later chapters or for missed major items; make corrections before finalizing the index.
